Part Three of the First Section: The Fundamental Chronicle of the Lord Śākyamuni Buddha.
Turning the Wheel of Dharma; Turning the Wheel of Dharma.
The Preface states:
To expound the Dharma and deliver sentient beings is the primary purpose for which the Tathāgata appears in the world.
Since individuals possess either sharp or dull faculties,
the Dharma accordingly has both sudden and gradual approaches; thus,
there is no one who hears the Dharma who does not attain realization and entry.
It is like a king of physicians who prescribes medicine according to the ailment;
if the medicine is suitable,
there is no illness that cannot be cured.
Does the Commentary not say:
"Now, from beginning to end, the Buddha fully turns the Dharma wheels of the five flavors;
by turning these dharmas to guide others, he causes their minds to attain awakening."
This is the meaning of turning the wheel of Dharma.
When the Tathāgata turned the wheel of Dharma,
he did so throughout five periods during his single lifetime.
Thus, there are eight teachings.
Regarding the "turning of the wheel of Dharma," the wheel takes the sense of crushing and grinding.
The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma,
transforming the minds of sentient beings and possessing mastery over all phenomena.
Just as the wheel-treasure of a universal monarch rolls forward without obstruction,
so too are the Tathāgata’s three wheels inconceivable:
namely, the wheel of the body, which manifests supernatural transformations.
The wheel of speech preaches the Dharma;
the wheel of mind discerns the capacities of beings.
Thus, it is able to crush and grind away all the afflictions and burdens of sentient beings.
The Fayuan states:
There are two types of wheel-turning kings. First, the wheel-turning king of material wealth (*cakravartin*).
There are four kinds of equality.
The golden wheel has a thousand spokes,
and its transformative influence covers the four continents.
He appears during the eon of abiding when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years;
his silver wheel has seven hundred and fifty spokes,
and he transforms the three continents.
Excluding the northern continent,
the copper wheel has five hundred spokes and transforms the two continents of the southeast.
The iron wheel has two hundred and fifty spokes;
it transforms only the southern continent,
as was the case with King Aśoka.
The Wheel-Turning King refers to the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world when the human lifespan has decreased from one hundred years.
"One generation" refers to this.
Generally, it refers to the eight aspects;
specifically, it pertains to the five periods.
Furthermore, within these five periods, there are both general and specific distinctions.
The *Myōhen* states: "Regarding the five flavors and the provisional and perfect [teachings],
it is discussed that each has its own distinct limits."
The Treatise on Penetration applies to both the beginning and the end.
If the Avataṃsaka Sūtra were specific, it would apply only to the beginning;
if it is general, it extends to the end.
The examples concerning the Deer Park and so forth have already been addressed accordingly.
Now, this treatise discusses the single transformation [of the Buddha] solely from the perspective of its distinct meanings.
Regarding the discussion of the five periods:
The meaning is derived from three sutras:

The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states: "The four teachings, such as the *Āgama* (Tripitaka), etc."
It comprehensively encompasses all Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras;
the causes and effects are clearly elucidated,

Each is tailored to the specific capacities and conditions [of beings], complete from beginning to end,
and does not exceed these four.
The four teachings, beginning with the Sudden,
are merely the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata,
which arranges the *pitakas* and so forth.
It harmonizes the waxing and waning of conditions to bring sentient beings to maturity;
it refutes the heterodox and establishes the orthodox, leading those of the Small Vehicle back to the Great;
and by abolishing the partial and revealing the perfect, it reunites the provisional with the ultimate.
There are various schools that maintain the five flavors arise from one another;
they benefit sentient beings without fixed method, appearing or withdrawing according to the times.
Regarding these "five periods":
First, regarding the *Huayan* [period]:
its full title is the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*.
The title is established by fully incorporating the person, the dharma, and a metaphor.
The *Bie xing xuanyi* states:
"Mahāvaipulya" refers to the Dharma;
"Buddha" refers to Vairocana, the person who has realized the fruit.
The *Avataṃsaka* is likened to the causes adorned by flowers that bring about the fruit of meritorious virtues; this scripture consists of seven locations and nine assemblies,
and as the venues for these assemblies are not uniform,
the title of the scripture is used to designate it.
Second, regarding the period at the Deer Park:
the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
stating that when the Tathāgata was on the causal ground, he served as the leader of a herd of deer.
The King of Vārāṇasī entered the mountains to hunt.
There was a doe carrying a fawn who was scheduled by turn to provide food for his meals.
The mother informed the Lord of Deer that her son had been killed unjustly;
the Lord of Deer then went to the king to beg for his life in exchange.
The King spoke in verse:
"I am truly a man-headed deer;
you are a deer-headed man."
One becomes a human being by virtue of principle,
not by virtue of physical form.
From this day forward, I [shall act accordingly].
I do not eat any meat;
I bestow this gift of fearlessness,
which may also bring peace to your mind.
It was inhabited by herds of deer,
and was therefore named the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva); it was also called the Pomegranate Garden (Āmrapālīvana).
It is named after its establishment;
it is also called the "Garden of the Rishis" because it was the dwelling place of two rishis.
This name is designated according to its location, commemorating the site where the causes for past practices were fulfilled.
During the period of the Threefold Vaipulya, the four teachings were expounded together; thus it is called "Vaipulya" (fang), meaning "square" or "even."
The phrase "equally benefiting the four capacities" and so forth is named after its dharma;
it is established based on the teachings of the [Mahāsāṃghika] school.
Therefore, the *Xuyiji* states:
"The name 'Vaipulya' (fangdeng) has two meanings.
If one follows the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is like producing fresh butter from curd."
This is like the *sūtras* emerging from the Vaipulya;
this refers to the third period,
specifically according to the teachings of that division.
This refers precisely to those with the capacities for the three vehicles and four teachings.
If one contemplates this Vaipulya Sūtra through the perspective of Samantabhadra,
it is the eye of all Buddhas.
This directly clarifies the perfect principle;
it is not of the third period. The term "Vaipulya" (fang-ping) refers to the meaning of vastness and equality.
Among all Mahāyāna sections, wherever the perfect principle is discussed, [it pertains to this].
These are both called Vaipulya.
During the fourth period, that of Prajñā,
this term is translated as "wisdom."
Among the five reasons for not translating [Sanskrit terms], this falls under "not translating due to its nobility.
The full name is *Mahāprajñā*.
This is the title derived from the scripture itself.
Regarding the fifth period, that of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa*,
these two sutras equally clarify the revelation and manifestation [of the Buddha-nature], both belonging to the stage of *amṛta* (the finest essence).
Therefore, they are combined into a single period.
These titles are all derived from the sūtra itself.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is fully titled the *Sūtra of the Lotus of the Sublime Dharma*.
This is because the "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*) possesses the threefold meaning of bestowing, revealing, and setting aside.
Therefore, the lotus flower is used as a metaphor.
As for *nirvāṇa*,
the full title is the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
This is translated as "Great Parinirvāṇa.
"Great" refers to the Dharma-body;
"extinction" refers to liberation.
The *Dù* (Sūtra on Deliverance) is identical to Prajñā; from its beginning to its end,
it speaks exclusively of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
These constitute the five periods.
The names established for these five periods do not transcend three meanings.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, the name is derived from a metaphor.
The Deer Park follows from the place;
the Vaipulya, Prajñā, and Nirvāṇa follow from the Dharma;
the Lotus Sūtra follows from both the Dharma and the parable.
It is also called the five flavors.
These possess two meanings: mutual generation and varying intensity (thick and thin).
Regarding "mutual generation":
The *Miaoxuan* states:
"After the initial sudden [teaching],
next the gradual [teaching] is opened."
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"From the Buddha emerge the twelve divisions of the scriptures;
from the twelve divisions of the scriptures emerges the *Sūtra*."
It is like milk coming from a cow, and curd coming from milk, and so forth;
they arise sequentially, without regard for whether they are thick or thin.
It further says:
That which is called "milk" does not have its essence in its lack of flavor;
it is so named because it is the beginning and the source.
Regarding the terms "intense" and "dilute," the *Yili* (Exemplary Meanings) states:
"The five flavors within the sutras."
This is merely an analogy for the varying degrees of intensity across the five periods of a single lifetime;
though the intensities differ, all emerge from the same cow.
Yuan Caotang said:

The teaching is illustrated by the analogy of mutual production; the capacities [of sentient beings] are illustrated by the analogy of varying degrees of intensity. Thus, the teaching possesses a sequential order.
From the sudden opening comes the gradual;
through the gradual, one enters ever deeper until finally converging upon the Perfect.
Thus, as for the capacities [of sentient beings], there are degrees of superiority and inferiority.
At the outset, he rebuked and refined those who were like the deaf and mute;
yet, in the end, the text for attaining the prediction consists of only one set of five flavors presented in two rounds of analogies.
While the analogies themselves are universal, that which they illustrate is specific.
Now, this treatise discusses the sequence of a single transformation, taking only the meaning of the arising of characteristics.

Regarding the four metaphors of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the *Myōgen* (*Miaofa lianhua jing xuanyi*) combines these four into three; the *Shakushaku* (*Fahua wenju shiqian*) opens these three into five; the *Avataṃsaka* takes the capacities of the audience as the basis for five; the *Myōgen* posits five periods; the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* posits five flavors; and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* posits five metaphors.

Regarding the names and meanings of the eight teachings:
To speak directly, that which addresses the Great [Vehicle] at the outset is called "sudden" (dun).
The three stages of flavor in the interim that lead those of the Small [Vehicle] toward the Great are called "gradual" (jian).
When different understandings arise from a single sound such that they do not recognize one another, it is called "secret" (guhya).
When hearing the Small [Vehicle] one realizes the Great, and hearing the Great one realizes the Small, it is called "indeterminate" (aniyata).
The Dharma and its meaning contained within the three—Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—are called the "Three Piṭakas" (tripiṭaka).

and is therefore called "Distinct" (Bie).
The teachings, wisdom, principle, severance, practice, stages, cause, and fruit are all perfectly interfused;
therefore, it is called "Perfect" (Yuan).

One cannot expect a complete analogy for even a small portion, as the *Śāstra* says:
The *Avataṃsaka* section represents the first flavor;
however, one has not yet attained the sudden teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*, nor its two distinct teachings of Separate and Perfect [Vehicles].
One should understand that this text merely presents the characteristics of the sequential order of the five flavors.
To say that the *Avataṃsaka* is like milk refers precisely to the intention of establishing the work of conversion by opening up the gradual from the sudden;
it was designed for those of appropriate capacity during the twenty-one days.
The commentary states:
Regarding the various texts that claim the "three times seven days" (twenty-one days) is intended for those of limited capacity,
there is no disagreement among people.
However, the *Xuánwén* states:
"In its initial portion, there are never any śrāvakas;
in its latter portion, however, there are."
Although he sat there as if deaf and mute,
the scholar Yishenzhi (義神智) refuted this on that basis, stating:
"The initial division is eternally non-existent."
What could possibly be compared to it?
Now, I shall explain this through two meanings to fully exhaust its principle.
First, during the initial phase of the three-week period, it is eternally non-existent.
This is the Tathāgata’s intention for transformative teaching according to what is appropriate.
Second, in the latter part [of his life],
he appeared as if deaf and mute.
This is the Tathāgata’s transformative activity according to what is appropriate for those to be guided.
First, regarding the intent behind this transformation, as stated in the "Expedient Means" chapter: "When he first sat at the site of enlightenment, he reflected for twenty-one days."
The divination stick says:
"During the first seven days, he contemplated preaching the Perfect [Teaching];
during the next seven days, he contemplated preaching the Separate [Teaching]."
For twenty-one days he contemplated preaching the *Abhisamaya*,
but because there were none with the capacity [to understand it], he taught only the Tripitaka.
The *Jian* (Sub-commentary) further states:
Regarding those of great capacity, it is the time at the site of enlightenment;
regarding those of small capacity, it is the time after [the Buddha] had completed his contemplation but before he had yet spoken. As Miaole says:
Those with limited vision perceive him as remaining for twenty-one days;
those with great vision see that from beginning to end there is no change.
These are all the Buddha’s transformative intentions, tailored to suit the capacities of beings.
Regarding the "transformative matters," as the text states:
"At the final session of the Avataṃsaka, the gradual [teachings] first began to unfold."
Miaole (Jiaoyi) explains it as follows:
"The old translation states:
'The Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, having entered the Lion-Stretching Samādhi.'"
Śāriputra emerged from the Jeta Grove,
yet he did not see the Tathāgata’s sovereign adornments,
nor did he see the assembly of the great bodhisattvas.
Those without the eye of wisdom are unable to see it,
nor can they offer praise;
this is what is meant by the phrase "like one who is deaf and mute."

Regarding that final assembly, it will indeed mark the gradual beginning of the teachings; now, examining the words of the Second Patriarch, they all indicate that those who are deaf and mute are in the latter part of the gradual teaching.
It is clearly understood, therefore, that this refers to the twelve years at the Deer Park.

For example, the *Myōhon* (Excellence of the Profound) states that the *Vaipulya* (fangděng) period of censure and rebuke should have occurred before the twelve years [of the *Āgama* teachings]. Inferring from this,
we know that the final assembly at the Jeta Grove was precisely the occasion for which the Tathāgata intended to provide the appropriate teaching.
Because the śrāvakas had previously practiced the Hīnayāna and were not yet capable of hearing the Mahāyāna—
being like those who are deaf and mute—
the Vimalakīrti was employed as a pretext to stimulate their progress.
This, then, is precisely what should be rebuked;
both cases fall within the twelve-year period,
and there is no room for doubt.

The *Sijiaoyi* (Outline of the Four Teachings) states that those who are deaf and mute are addressed in the *Avataṃsaka*, while those who are rebuked and censured are addressed in the *Vaipulya*. This, however,
is discussed solely in terms of the specific divisions within the scriptures.
In fact, this is not the correct interpretation.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"May the Bodhisattvas, such as Guangming (Light-Radiance) and others..."
Each spoke ten verses to exhort the śrāvakas.
The first verse rebuked them, saying:
All the pratyekabuddhas and those great śrāvakas are entirely unable to know the sphere of the bodhisattva’s practice;
this is the passage from the latter section that subsumes under the preceding example, and it all pertains to the transformative activities adapted to specific capacities.
Those of former times were unable to distinguish between various texts;
not understanding the Buddha’s intention behind his transformations nor the events of those transformations,
they viewed them all as a confused whole.
Consequently, there are many differing accounts.
As for the "Seven Locations and Eight Assemblies," this refers to the sixty-fascicle version of the old translation.
Translated by Buddhabhadra of the Jin dynasty;
this is the version cited by Tiantai,
as opposed to the eighty-fascicle new translation.
This was translated by Śikṣānanda of the Tang dynasty.
With the addition of the single assembly of Universal Radiance,
these constitute the seven locations and nine assemblies.
There are thirty-nine chapters.
Only the "Inconceivable Number of Minor Marks and Radiance" was spoken by the Buddha;
all the others were spoken through the empowerment of various bodhisattvas.
The First Assembly:

The Six Chapters Spoken at the Site of Enlightenment. At the site of enlightenment in the A-raṇya forest of Magadha, the World-Honored One, the Subtly Adorned by the Sovereigns of the World, first attained perfect awakening.
Jingxi said: "Since this differs from the long-established [teachings on] lifespan,
it is not the same as [the account in] the Āgamas regarding [the Buddha's realization] beneath the Bodhi tree."

Spontaneously abiding in the traces [of the path] refers to the Separate and Perfect Teachings (*bhedavaiṣamyasamyak-saṃbhinnayāna*). When the Tathāgata manifested his marks, the Buddha of the High Mark had a bodhisattva who spoke a verse, saying:
The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm.
[Thus it continues: Samantabhadra-samādhi; Samantabhadra enters the Tathāgata-garbha-atom-samādhi;
he manifests atom-sized Buddha-fields and worlds, accomplishing the Samantabhadra-exposition on the accomplishment of worlds.
Possessing ten matters and ten causal conditions, Samantabhadra expounded the Flower Treasury World-Ocean;
like the distribution of a celestial net, it is securely established in space. Vairocana’s Samantabhadra then spoke of the names of the Buddhas within this world-system.
In the old sutras, Śākyamuni is also named Rocana,
whereas in the new sutras he is named Vairocana. Miaole says:
"That the Dharma and its fruition are not divided into two or three and cannot be distinguished" refers precisely to this.
This is the second assembly.

In the Hall of Universal Radiance at the Site of Enlightenment, six chapters were taught: the "Names of the Tathāgatas," in which Mañjuśrī speaks of the names of the Buddhas in the worlds of the ten directions; the "Four Noble Truths," in which Mañjuśrī explains the names and meanings of the Four Truths; the "Awakening of Radiance," in which Mañjuśrī speaks in verse to praise the Buddha’s emission of light; the "Questions of the Bodhisattvas," in which the Bodhisattvas inquire about the meaning of awakening; and the "Destruction of Ignorance," in which Mañjuśrī questions Vijñaptimātratā-praveśa (Jue-shou) and others regarding the meaning of the destruction of ignorance.
The Bodhisattva Dharmottara said:
"It is like a person who counts another's treasures,
yet possesses not even half a coin for himself."
One who does not practice the Dharma,
though they may be widely learned, is just like this:
like a person who possesses excellent prescriptions and medicines.
Unable to save oneself from one's own illness,
it is like a deaf person performing music:
they delight others but do not hear it themselves.
Furthermore, the *Bhadramukha* states:
"The one who is unimpeded in all things,
the single path for transcending birth and death"— this was the pure prose response of Mañjuśrī to Jñānacakra.
Regarding all practices and vows:
when eating a meal, one should wish that sentient beings take the joy of dhyāna as their food.
Filled with the Joy of Dharma. All the verses originate from this chapter. Wenshu (Mañjuśrī) asked Xianshou (Bhadramukha) about the merits of the bodhicitta and so forth:
"Faith is the source of the Path and the mother of merit."
The Third Assembly:
Six chapters were preached in the Palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
○ Ascending Mount Sumeru, the Buddha sat beneath the Bodhi tree.
Without rising from this seat, he ascended Mount Sumeru.
Śakra praised him, saying,
"Kāśyapa once came and dwelt in this palace."
Therefore, this place is most auspicious.
Thus, in praise according to the ten Buddhas of the past,
they all declared that this place is most auspicious.
Jingxi said: "Ascending without moving;
responding to the capacity [of beings] to reach the mountain peak, he praises the Buddha seated in Indra’s Hall with verses."
The ten bodhisattvas, beginning with Dharmamati, each spoke a verse in praise of the Buddha’s supreme wisdom, saying:
"He thoroughly understands that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature."
Understanding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) in this way, one sees how Vairocana, in his Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), expounds the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*).

In each abode, he exhorts the cultivation of ten dharmas; Dharmaprajñā explains that there are ten dharmas for the cultivation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*); and Dharmaprajñā answers Śakra’s questions regarding the merit of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
The merit of generating the aspiration for enlightenment is such that it ensures the lineage of the Buddhas remains unbroken,
and through a single thought-moment, one knows the vast worlds and their long and short kalpas.
Because there are Buddhas and there are no Buddhas; because there is one Buddha and there are many Buddhas;
because in a single thought-moment one knows the kalpas of formation and destruction of the worlds throughout the three periods of time;
and because of the various distinctions among sentient beings.
Jingxi said: "The object of focus for the arousal of the bodhicitta is the realm of contemplation;
it possesses the three truths and is empty of intrinsic nature."

Within the equality of all conventional designations, the Wisdom of Dharmas elucidates how a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment, by abandoning the ten forms of negligence and practicing ten kinds of dharmas, possesses great merit and accomplishes the wisdom of a Buddha.
Jingxi said: "Enlightenment" refers to that which is realized;
"Dharma" refers to the method.

The Fourth Assembly. In the Palace of the Yāma Heaven, four chapters were spoken. The Buddha ascended to the Yāma Heaven; the Buddha was invited into the hall by the King of Yāma; the King of Yāma praised him with verses; the assembly of Bodhisattvas, beginning with Guṇakaraṇḍavyūha, each spoke verses in praise of the Buddha.
A verse from the *Juelin* (Forest of Enlightenment) says:
"The mind is like a skillful painter,
creating all manner of the five aggregates."
Within all the worlds,
nothing surpasses name and form.
It is also said:
As is the mind, so too is the Buddha;
as is the Buddha, so too are sentient beings. Thus, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are non-dual.
These three are without distinction.
Furthermore, if a person wishes to fully understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, [they should know this].
One should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm:
that all things are created solely by the mind. This is taught in the Ten Practices and Merit Forests and the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries Forests.
Fifth Assembly.

The Exposition of the Three Grades in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace. Ascending to Tuṣita Heaven. The Buddha ascends to this heaven; the assembly requests the Buddha to enter the palace. Praise in Verse in Tuṣita. Vajradhvaja and others praise the Buddha with ten verses on the Ten Dedications. Vajradhvaja speaks a verse, saying:
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) pervades all places;
all sentient beings and lands throughout the three periods of time are entirely contained within it, without exception.
Furthermore, no form or characteristic can be apprehended.
This is the sixth assembly,
where one chapter is taught in the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, spoken by Vajragarbha regarding the Ten Stages.
The ten stages (bhūmis) are correlated with the various heavenly kings,
just as the Radiant Stage (Prabhākārī-bhūmi) is correlated with the Heavenly King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and so forth.
This is the seventh major assembly.

In the Hall of Universal Radiance, eleven chapters were taught: Samantabhadra of the Ten Concentrations spoke on entering the ten kinds of samādhi; Samantabhadra of the Ten Supernatural Powers spoke on the ten kinds of supernatural powers; Samantabhadra of the Ten Endurances spoke on the ten kinds of endurance; and for the Bodhisattva Mind-King, incalculable Buddhas [spoke].
He spoke of *asaṃkhyeya*, the immeasurable, up to the unspeakably unspeakable number of eons (*kalpa*), praising the infinite lifespan and the qualities of Samantabhadra;
the Mind-King Sūtra on Comparison Spoke of the Length and Shortness of World-Eons; and the Mind-King Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Abodes Spoke of Mount Qingliang in the Northeast.
It is the dwelling place of Mañjuśrī and ten thousand bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, it is said that in the land of China there is the Nārāyaṇa Cave, where the Buddha’s Inconceivable Lotus Treasury Bodhisattva expounded the "Inconceivable Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata's Wondrous Virtue," and Samantabhadra expounded the "Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata."
Each [of these] possesses the major marks and minor signs of a Tathāgata, with as many rays of light as there are atoms in ten Flower Treasury World-Oceans. The Buddha said to Ratnapāṇi:
"I shall describe how the light from these minor signs illuminates world-systems as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields."
Those in the hells encounter light and their suffering ceases;

they are all reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven. The Universal Worthy Practice was taught by Universal Worthy. The Cultivation of the Ten Dharmas and so forth was taught by the Tathāgata’s Appearance. The Buddha emits light named “The Appearance of the Tathāgata. The Vairocana Fundamental Vow was taught by Universal Worthy.
The eighth assembly:
In the Hall of Universal Radiance, one chapter was preached, titled "Leaving the World," in which Samantabhadra extensively enumerates the various practices of bodhisattvas.
The ninth assembly.

In the Jeta Grove, one chapter is taught, namely the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden. At the time of entering the Dharma-realm, the World-Honored One entered the Lion’s Yawn Samādhi, while Śāriputra and the other great śrāvakas were in the Jeta Grove.
None of them perceived the supernatural power of the Tathāgata,
nor did they see the great assembly of bodhisattvas,
because their roots of goodness were not the same.
They did not originally cultivate the roots of goodness for seeing the Buddha;
they did not originally praise or speak of the miraculous transformations of the Buddhas,
and thus were unable to see, hear, or recollect them.
Because one attains liberation by relying on the vehicle of hearing [the Dharma]. At that time, Mañjuśrī took his leave of the Buddha and traveled south toward the human realm.
Then Śāriputra, together with six thousand bhikṣus, went to where Mañjuśrī was.
Mañjuśrī exhorted him with ten matters,
causing him to practice the bodhisattva path;
he immediately attained the unimpeded eye samādhi.
He beheld the realm of all Buddhas and saw all the Buddhas.
Thus did Mañjuśrī exhort him.
Traveling south, he arrived at the eastern side of Puṇyavatī City and preached the Dharma for the youth Sudhana,
causing him to seek awakening and draw near to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
From here, traveling south for one hundred and ten cities,
he encountered fifty-three spiritual friends.
Entering the Samantabhadra Bodhimanda,

one attains samādhi-gates as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields and perceives Samantabhadra everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions. (This is all extracted from Jingxi’s *Huayan Gumu*).
The divination slip states:
"There are three versions preserved in the Dragon Palace;
the superior version consists of as many chapters as there are atoms in thirteen world-systems."
The middle version consists of 498,800 verses;
the abbreviated version consists of 100,000 verses in forty-eight chapters,
whereas the present version contains only thirty-nine chapters.
Thus we know that the transmission of the sutra was not yet complete; Nāgārjuna entered the Dragon Palace to consult the scriptures,
and because the upper and middle versions were not fit for the world,
he recited only the lower version to circulate in the world.
On the ninth day of the second month,
for seven days, the Tathāgata contemplated the King of Trees with single-minded concentration,
and thought to himself:
The Dharma I have attained is extremely profound and difficult to understand;
only a Buddha and a Buddha can know it.
All sentient beings possess meager merit and dull faculties.
"How can they understand the Dharma I have attained?
I would rather enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Great Brahmā Deva King...
He immediately departed from his celestial palace and arrived at the place where the Tathāgata was, saying:
"World-Honored One."
Having begun now, you shall achieve the unsurpassed path.
Why do you remain silent and not preach the Dharma?
For there are sentient beings who, having planted various roots of virtue in past lives, are capable of hearing the Dharma.
We only pray that the World-Honored One, for their sake,
shall turn the sublime wheel of Dharma through the power of great compassion.
It is the same for Śakra Devānām Indra up to the gods of the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations.
At that time, from the Brahma King down to others, they made their request three times;
after seven days had passed,
[the Buddha] accepted it in silence.
During the second seven-day period,
he observed all sentient beings with his Buddha-eye, discerning their superior, middling, and inferior faculties as well as their various afflictions.
During the third seven-day period, he engaged in contemplation.
"Now I shall open the gate of the Dharma of Immortality.
Who shall be the first to hear it? Ārāḍa made this vow.
Before he had completed the Way,
there was a voice in the air saying,
"He passed away yesterday."
He further reflected that Kālaṇḍaka, being of sharp faculties,
should also have heard it first; yet,
a voice spoke again from the sky, saying, "He passed away last night."
He further reflected that the five men sent by the king and his ministers had made a vow in the past that they should be the first to hear the Dharma.
He immediately rose from his seat and went to Vārāṇasī.
According to the *Caiguo jing* (Sūtra on Cause and Effect) cited in the *Wenju* (Commentary on the Text),
the [period of] twenty-one days is no different from that in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Furthermore, the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan fuxing zhuanhong jue*) extensively cites various sutras to demonstrate that the three-week periods [of mourning] are all different;
only the *Inaguo jing* (Sutra on Cause and Effect) roughly accords with the intention of our Master.
Therefore, the records of the Buddha today are largely based on this sutra.
As for the two seers, Ārāḍa and Udraka Rāmaputra:
Including the five disciples headed by Cunda;
these are recorded together in the second fascicle of the Benji (Basic Annals).
On the thirtieth day of the second month.
The World-Honored One went to the waterside of the blind nāga Mucilinda and sat for seven days;
his radiance illuminated the water.
The dragon’s eyes were opened.
He remembered his previous vision of the radiance of the three Buddhas within the Bhadrakalpa: Krakucchanda, [Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa].
The Anāgāmin Kāśyapa,
who possessed the three kinds of buddhahood, was able to see as soon as he opened his eyes;
he then emerged from the water and beheld the Buddha.
It rained for seven days;
the dragon coiled his body around him seven times,
and with his seven heads spread out like a canopy, he provided a protective shelter.
When the rain ceased after seven days, the Buddha arose from his meditative absorption.

The dragon transformed himself into a young man practitioner, and the Buddha immediately conferred upon him the Dharma of the Three Refuges, just as Trapusa and Bhallika had taken refuge in the future Sangha; this was the first instance among all animals of seeing the Buddha, according to the *Caiguo jing* (Sutra on the Causes and Effects).
On the seventh day of the third month, the tree deity knew that the Buddha had sat down by this water for seven days; however, it was not the Bodhi-tree deity who had yet offered him food.
Just then, five hundred merchants were passing by from the side of the mountain;
their carts and oxen all stumbled and could not move forward, emitting a sound like *qù* (the same as *nǎi*).
He was obstructed and unable to proceed.
Before him and behind him were two great men, Tiwei and...
[the text is incomplete].
Pāli and [the other] went together to the tree deity and requested a blessing.
The tree deity then spoke for them.
The Buddha was by the water's edge.
"It would be fortunate for you all to offer food first," they said.
The two men then mixed honey with parched grain and presented it to the Buddha.
The Four Heavenly Kings took stone bowls that had appeared spontaneously within the rocks, each offering one to present to the Buddha.
According to the *Caiguo jing* (Sutra on Cause and Effect), the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Manifestation of the Buddha) states:
"Each of the Four Heavenly Kings offered a bowl made of blue stone. The Buddha considered taking only one bowl, but he did not wish to displease the other kings."
He then took all four bowls,
stacked them in his left hand,
and pressed them together with his right hand until they became a single bowl.
He caused those at the four borders to see the auspicious response; the Buddha then offered a blessing for them.
When they had finished eating, he immediately conferred the Three Refuges upon the merchants:
first, taking refuge in the Buddha.
Second, taking refuge in the Dharma;
third, taking refuge in the Sangha of the future. In the *Sutra on Cause and Effect*, the Buddha first explained for them the five elements, the six stems, and the calculations of yin and yang.
Once they were convinced and had gained faith, he caused them to take refuge in the Buddha.
He took refuge in the Dharma and took refuge in the future Sangha.
At that time, the elder attained the stage of Srotāpanna— this is called one who has entered the stream, the first fruit— and [the Buddha] further preached the five precepts to him, saying:
The five precepts are the mother of all Buddhas;
those who seek the Buddha-way should read this sutra.
When those seeking the fruit of Arhatship— known here as the "Unborn"— the fourth of the noble fruits, read this sutra,
Tiwei attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti),
and three hundred people attained the patience of faith (śraddhā-kṣānti).
Two hundred people attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
Five hundred merchants and the Four Heavenly Kings attained the *anulomikī-dharma-kṣānti*. (From the *Tiwei jing*). [Supplementary Note:
According to the *Sanbao lu*, this is recorded as such.
Originally there was one fascicle of the *Tiewei jing*.
Later, during the Wei dynasty, Tanjing compiled the two-fascicle *Tiewei bolijing*,
adding the Five Elements and the Five Directions.
It is further stated:
"In the east is Mount Tai;
in the language of Han, it is called Dàyuè."
Not recognizing the translations of the Fan and Wei dynasties,
later generations came to regard it as spurious;
one should instead rely on the single-fascicle version.
For the sake of the Buddha Zhengfo (Correct Buddha) and Tiwei,
he bestowed a prediction that they would attain Buddhahood in the future,
with the names Tathāgata Mijian (Secret Accomplishment) and Rulai Puyao (Universally Radiant).
This is attributed to Tiwei.
The commentary states:
"The Buddha taught the five precepts as the teaching for humans and devas."
This is precisely what is revealed:
that Tiwei attained patience upon hearing the Small Vehicle [teachings] yet realized the Great Vehicle;
this is indeed the "indeterminate" [nature].
This constitutes the explicit teaching of the indeterminate [turning of the wheel].
If reckoned by time, it occurs after the thirty-seven days of the *Avataṃsaka* and after the seven days at the water's edge.
This is the fifth seven-day period.
As stated in the *Caoyin jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions):
"If one were to collect the scriptures, they comprise the teachings for humans and devas."
It is subsumed within the Tripitaka,
as stated in the *Sijiaoyi* (The Meaning of the Four Teachings).
Next, regarding the gradual teaching, there are three periods.
The Deer Park represents the initial stage of gradual teaching; the Vaipulya represents the middle stage of gradual teaching;
and the Prajñāpāramitā represents the final stage of gradual teaching.
These are collectively termed the "Gradual Teachings.
The commentary states:
These were of no benefit for the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* because they were intended for a specific class of limited-capacity practitioners, such as Śāriputra and others.
Having opened the way through the sudden [teaching], they were gradually led in sequence;
first, at the Deer Park, they equally realized the minor fruits of the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
This was followed by the intermediate Vaipulya [teachings].
Discarding the partial and rejecting the minor [vehicles], they collectively aspire to the Great Dharma.
Gradually reaching the end of Prajñā,
they turn the teaching and entrust the inheritance, thereby understanding the family estate.
Therefore, it is collectively termed "gradual.
Regarding the second period, that of the Deer Park:
the Buddha originally intended to deliver sentient beings by means of the Mahāyāna.
Those who were unable [to proceed] immediately sought a means to travel to Vārāṇasī— here called Jiangraocheng—
which lies within the borders of Central India.
In the Deer Park within the city, he differentiated the teaching of the One Vehicle by expounding it as three;
this is precisely the opening of the Tripiṭaka teachings.
It was not only Śākyamuni who concealed his immeasurable divine virtues to effect such gradual transformation.
The Buddhas of the past and future are likewise so.
One should know that after the initial sudden [teaching], the gradual is subsequently opened;
for those with gradual capacities, the sudden is fully produced within them, just as milk [is produced from curds].
Within the Tripitaka, the transformation from the ordinary to the sagely is likened to the change of milk into curd;

these arise in succession, and one does not take the thick or thin [stages] as the profound and subtle [truth], for they are of no benefit for the sudden [teaching] regarding the three vehicles of root-nature.
Without moving from the tranquil site of enlightenment, he roamed the Deer Park;
he cast off his precious and noble robes of *śānta* and donned the tattered, filthy garments of six feet.

Previously, for the sake of the five bhikṣus, he taught the matters of the Four Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the Six Perfections, and so forth—the teachings of the four methods [of conversion]. (From the *Fourfold Ritual of the Teachings*) The *Wenju* says:
"The past is called the 'root' (*mūla*);
the future is called the 'nature' (*prakṛti*). This is the great contained within the small."
Therefore, it is called "immovable.
The sublime, distinguished, and supreme response-body is adorned with meditative concentration and wisdom,
comparable to precious and noble garments.
The physical body of the Inferior Response [Buddha] endures the afflictions of birth and phenomena;
it is likened to a soiled garment.
The Buddha was born among human beings.
Twice as superior to the human form,
his height is one zhang and six chi;
this is like when Maitreya is thirty-two zhang tall, whereas the people of that time will be sixteen zhang tall.
If considered in terms of time, it is like the subtle and profound illumination of a dark valley; if considered in terms of flavor, it is like the production of curd from milk.
This [text] emerges from the twelve divisions of the scriptures as the ninth division, the Sūtras, which are subtle and profound.
The *Śraddhāparivarta* states:

"At that time, the elder, wishing to entice his son back, having ceased his grand display, did not wish to abandon him alone; he secretly dispatched two men, concealing their true identities for the sake of secrecy."

The employment of skillful means (*upāya*) serves as the dismissal. Below this are instances of inference (*anumāna*): furthermore, on another day, seeing from within a window that [the child] was situated in a narrow space and observing his body from afar—being at a great distance—is "seeing from afar"; and describing him as "emaciated" refers to his being haggard and withered due to having little wisdom or merit.

His *zhàng-lù* (sixteen-foot) form is "coarse."
The two types of patience regarding phenomena and sentient beings are essential.

This means that cold, heat, wind, rain, and so forth belong to the category of phenomena; by using the coarse, vulgar, and common right hand to hold the vessel for removing filth, one treats the phenomena of outflows (*āsrava*) consisting of the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
The left hand symbolizes reality, while the right hand symbolizes expedient means. He addressed all the laborers: "My children, work diligently;
set your minds at ease."
I am like your father, appearing as a semblance but not yet real;

you, from this point forward, shall be like a son born of me, approaching the True and drawing near to the Holy—the stage of the World’s First Dharma. At that time, though the impoverished son rejoices at this encounter, [he remains unaware].

Even so, he still considered himself a lowly hired laborer, knowing himself unworthy to succeed to the great [lineage]; for twenty years he was constantly made to clear away dung, yet upon seeing the Truth, he attained liberation and the state of being unimpeded.
Contemplating the nine liberations and the nine unhindered knowledges together makes twenty.

That is to say, one uses the eight patiences and eight knowledges to sever the afflictions of the path of seeing,

On the eighth day of the third month,

First, the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path: the first two truths (suffering and its origin) constitute the worldly cause and effect—the fruit of suffering and the cause of its accumulation—while the latter two truths (cessation and the path) constitute the supramundane cause and effect—the fruit of cessation and the cause of the path. The turning that demonstrates,

As it is said: "This is suffering; I have already known it, and there is nothing further to be known.

For the eight persons, including the Bodhisattva Bādhaka,
he preached the Pratyutpanna Sūtra clarifying the practice of austerities and the *Shier you jing* (Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings).
In the eleventh year, the Gengyin year, on the day Ānanda was ordained at the age of eight.

The full ordination (*upasampadā*) is obtained through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations); because this includes the preceding single motion (*jñapti*), it is called "white-four" (*bai-si*).
*Karman* is translated as "action," referring here to the wholesome action performed. He ordained one hundred and ten arhats.
He received the threefold formula of the precepts and first shaved off his beard and hair with a precious sword;
he then instructed Kauṇḍinya and the others.

Throughout the three worlds, he conferred the precepts upon the śrāmaṇeras according to the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya; in this year, the Buddha preached the Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings for King Cūḍapanthaka’s younger brother at Mount Liuyang.
